idiom_name: context manager protocol (__enter__/__exit__) + with statement; contextlib.closing / ExitStack
implementation_notes: Python's with statement is the language-level realization: an object that owns resources implements __enter__/__exit__ and __exit__ runs on every exit path, including exceptions raised in the block. contextlib fills the gaps - closing() adapts any object that merely has close(), @contextlib.contextmanager turns a generator with try/finally into a context manager, ExitStack composes several resources and unwinds them in reverse order, and asynccontextmanager/aclosing mirror this for async code. CPython's reference counting usually frees objects promptly, but prompt is not deterministic and __del__ is not a cleanup contract, so explicit release belongs in __exit__/close(); weakref.finalize is only a net. Cascade is manual: __exit__ releases the resources the object owns and leaves borrowed ones alone. An object whose lifetime exceeds one lexical scope exposes close()/aclose() and additionally supports the context manager protocol for the scoped case.
code_sketch:
class Session:
    def __init__(self, conn): self._conn, self._closed = conn, False
    def close(self):                         # idempotent cascade
        if not self._closed:
            self._closed = True; self._conn.close()
    def __enter__(self): return self
    def __exit__(self, *exc): self.close(); return False

with Session(connect()) as s:                # closed on every exit path
    s.round_trip()
pitfalls: __exit__ must not raise during normal cleanup: an exception escaping it replaces the in-flight one, and returning True suppresses the original exception instead of propagating it.
Context managers built with @contextmanager are one-shot: reusing the same object raises instead of re-running the cleanup.
A resource stored on a longer-lived object (self._session) is never released by the with block; it needs an explicit close(), and weakref.finalize only runs if no reference keeps it alive.
